advances: A concave-boundary test supplies an exact line-to-global canonical comparison without a coupling error proportional to the probability that the endpoints lie on different lines. For the actual minimum-area shrinking-mass cores and shortest reduced lattice vectors of the accepted normalization, this excludes every bounded nonvanishing score increment. The result isolates the unbounded-score branch of that direction. It does not establish the requested existence of a basis with vanishing score increments, and it supplies no quadrature or continuous-operator conclusion.

proof:
First prove (2). Write \(f(s)=\sup\{z:(s,z)\in K\}\) on the real first-coordinate projection of \(K\). Convexity implies that \(f\) is concave: the convex combination of two points on the upper boundary belongs to \(K\), so its second coordinate is at most the upper boundary at its first coordinate. For every support point \((i,j)\), define its nonnegative deficit \(d(i,j)=f(i)-j\), and set \(\varphi(i,j)=e^{-d(i,j)/2}\) and \(\psi(i,j)=\varphi(i,j)^2=e^{-d(i,j)}\). Both functions take values in \([0,1]\).

Use the canonical sampling representation from accepted fact `b09fd2c6d7d7ab1d`: choose the full parity class \(\mathbf B\) with its original mass \(\pi_{\mathbf b}\), choose conditionally independent \(\mathbf X,\mathbf Y\) from \(u\) in that class, and put \(\mathbf J=(\mathbf X+\mathbf Y)/2\). The support is complete, so \(\mathbf J\) is a support point. Concavity of \(f\) gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
d(\mathbf J)&\ge\frac{d(\mathbf X)+d(\mathbf Y)}2,\\
\psi(\mathbf J)&\le\varphi(\mathbf X)\varphi(\mathbf Y),\\
\mathbb E_u\psi-\mathbb E_{\mathcal T(u)}\psi
&\ge\sum_{\mathbf b}\pi_{\mathbf b}
\operatorname{Var}(\varphi(\mathbf X)\mid\mathbf B=\mathbf b).
\tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]

The last line follows by conditional independence and by writing \(\mathbb E_u\psi=\sum_{\mathbf b}\pi_{\mathbf b}\mathbb E[\varphi^2\mid\mathbf B=\mathbf b]\). Since \(\psi\) has oscillation at most one, its expectation difference is at most \(\operatorname{TV}(u,\mathcal T(u))\). Thus (3) is an exact global comparison; it does not compare \(\mathcal T(u)\) with a separate rowwise midpoint law.

Fix an occupied line \(i\), let its mass be \(a_i\), and let \(b_i\) be its largest integer second coordinate. Completeness gives a consecutive interval of sites. Write them as \((i,b_i-n)\), \(0\le n\le L_i\). The conditional probabilities on the line are \(\rho_n=\rho_0e^{-tn}\), with \(\rho_0=(\sum_{n=0}^{L_i}e^{-tn})^{-1}\ge1-e^{-t}\). Since \(b_i=\lfloor f(i)\rfloor\), the real number \(\phi_i=f(i)-b_i\) lies in \([0,1)\), and \(\varphi(i,b_i-n)=e^{-(\phi_i+n)/2}\).

If \(L_i\ge2\), consider the second-coordinate parity containing \(n=0\). Its conditional line mass is \(\beta_i=\sum_{n\ \mathrm{even}}\rho_n\le1\). The variance identity \(\operatorname{Var}(W)=\frac12\sum_{a,b}r_ar_b(W_a-W_b)^2\), applied to that parity-conditioned line law and retaining just the pair \(n=0,2\), gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\beta_i\operatorname{Var}(\varphi\mid i,\ n\ \mathrm{even})
&\ge\frac{\rho_0\rho_2}{\beta_i}
\left(e^{-\phi_i/2}-e^{-(\phi_i+2)/2}\right)^2\\
&\ge e^{-1}(1-e^{-1})^2\rho_0^2e^{-2t}\\
&\ge c_*(1-e^{-t})^2e^{-2t}.
\tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]

Conditioning further on the line index can only decrease the average conditional variance in (3), by the law of total variance. The weight of the indicated line and parity in that average is \(a_i\beta_i\). Summing (4) with weights \(a_i\) over the lines with at least three sites proves (2). The coordinate first parity is fixed on each line, so this calculation uses the full original-mass parity conditioning throughout. Integral affine lattice coordinate changes merely permute its four classes, as in `b09fd2c6d7d7ab1d`.

Now apply this comparison to the actual cores. Accepted fact `3f23ec160b160e93` gives \(1-\eta_k\le\alpha_k\), completeness of \(F_k\), and
\(B(\mathbf0,r)\subseteq A_kK_k\subseteq B(\mathbf0,R)\), where \(r=1/(3\sqrt2)\) and \(R=2\). Define the auxiliary law \(u_{k,\mathbf I}=p_{k,\mathbf I}/\alpha_k\) for \(\mathbf I\in F_k\), and zero otherwise. Its original tilt is still \(\boldsymbol\theta_k\), its largest atom is at most \(p_{\max,k}/(1-\eta_k)\), and \(\operatorname{TV}(p_k,u_k)=1-\alpha_k\le\eta_k\). The global canonical continuity inequality in accepted fact `b09fd2c6d7d7ab1d` therefore yields

\[
\operatorname{TV}(u_k,\mathcal T(u_k))
\le\operatorname{TV}(u_k,p_k)+\delta_k+
\operatorname{TV}(\mathcal T(p_k),\mathcal T(u_k))
\le\delta_k+4\eta_k.
\tag{5}
\]

For clarity, every coordinate and lattice map used next is exact. Put \(\mathbf v_{k,i}=G_k\mathbf g_{k,i}\). Because \(\mathbf g_{k,1},\mathbf g_{k,2}\) is a basis of \(G_k^{-1}\mathbb Z^2\), the vectors \(\mathbf v_{k,1},\mathbf v_{k,2}\) are a unimodular basis of \(\mathbb Z^2\). Moreover \(\boldsymbol\theta_k\cdot\mathbf v_{k,i}=\boldsymbol\lambda_k\cdot\mathbf g_{k,i}\). If necessary reverse \(\mathbf v_{k,1}\) and \(\mathbf g_{k,1}\) to make the first score nonnegative. In the case \(t_k>0\), use coordinates
\(\mathbf x=\mathbf u_{k,0}+i\mathbf v_{k,2}+j\mathbf v_{k,1}\). Then \(A_k\mathbf x=i\mathbf g_{k,2}+j\mathbf g_{k,1}-\mathbf c_\triangle\), and the score in the \(j\)-direction is exactly \(t_k\). The integer translation and unimodular linear part permute the original parity classes. Equivalently their transported cosets remain
\(G_k^{-1}(\mathbf b-\mathbf u_{k,0})-\mathbf c_\triangle+2\Gamma_k\), exactly as specified in `3f23ec160b160e93`; no standard-grid parity convention is imposed on \(\Gamma_k\).

It remains to bound the mass of lines containing fewer than three sites. Suppress the index \(k\). Let \(d_1=\|\mathbf g_1\|\) and \(h=|\det(\mathbf g_1,\mathbf g_2)|/d_1\). The shortest-vector and nearest-reduction argument in `3f23ec160b160e93` gives \(h\ge\sqrt3\,d_1/2\). The affine lattice lines parallel to \(\mathbf g_1\) have normal coordinates in an arithmetic progression of spacing \(h\).

Choose a unit normal \(\mathbf n\) to these lines. Let \([a,b]\) be the projection of \(AK\) onto \(\mathbf n\), and let \(\ell(s)\) be the Euclidean length of its chord on \(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf y=s\). Convexity implies concavity of \(\ell\): the convex combinations of the two chord intervals lie in the intervening chord, and the length of their interval combination is the same convex combination of their lengths. The ball inclusions give \(a\le-r<0<r\le b\), \(b\le R\), \(-a\le R\), and \(\ell(0)\ge2r\). Hence

\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell(s)&\ge\frac{2r}{R}(b-s) &&(0\le s\le b),\\
\ell(s)&\ge\frac{2r}{R}(s-a) &&(a\le s\le0).
\tag{6}
\end{aligned}
\]

A chord of length at least \(3d_1\) contains at least three points of its affine lattice line, because consecutive points on that line are exactly \(d_1\) apart. Completeness puts all these points in the core support. Thus an occupied line with at most two sites has \(\ell(s)<3d_1\). By (6), its normal coordinate lies in one of the two intervals of length \(3Rd_1/(2r)\) adjacent to \(a\) and \(b\). Each such interval contains at most \(\lceil\sqrt3 R/r\rceil+1=16\) of the line coordinates, since their spacing is \(h\ge\sqrt3 d_1/2\). There are consequently at most 32 short occupied lines. Each has at most two sites, so their total \(u\)-mass is at most \(64u_{\max}\). Therefore \(m_{\ge3}\ge[1-64u_{\max}]_+\).

Combining (2), (5), and this mass estimate proves (1) for \(t_k>0\). When \(t_k=0\), its right-hand side is zero, so (1) also holds. For any fixed \(0<\varepsilon<T<\infty\), a subsequence with \(t_k\in[\varepsilon,T]\) would make the right-hand side of (1) at least
\(c_*(1-e^{-\varepsilon})^2e^{-2T}(1-o(1))>0\), whereas its left-hand side tends to zero. This proves the asserted exclusion and the bounded-score conclusion.

The limitation concerning unbounded scores is substantive. For an interval law with probabilities proportional to \(e^{tj}\), \(0\le j\le L\), its top-site mass is at least \(1-e^{-t}\). In its canonical sampling, both endpoints have that interval law unconditionally, so the midpoint fails to be the top site with probability at most \(2e^{-t}\). The triangle inequality through the top-site point mass gives \(\operatorname{TV}(\rho,\mathcal T(\rho))\le3e^{-t}\), uniformly in \(L\). Thus even lines of arbitrarily many sites can have vanishing conditional canonical defect when \(t\to\infty\). This is not a counterexample to the root-law claim: those conditional interval laws have largest atom tending to one. It identifies why (2) alone cannot dispose of that branch when many lines make the global largest atom small. A further geometric comparison must control the contribution of pairs from different lines, or construct a different adapted basis. Also, the second vector of a nearest-reduced basis need not have its length bounded by a constant times its transverse line spacing, so the 32-line argument applies to the shortest vector as stated and does not assert the corresponding estimate for that second vector.
statement:
Let \(D_k\subseteq\mathbb Z^2\) be finite, complete, and of affine rank two, and let the original root law be \(p_{k,\mathbf I}=e^{\boldsymbol\theta_k\cdot\mathbf I}/Z_k\) on \(D_k\), extended by zero elsewhere. The exact aliases to accepted fact `b09fd2c6d7d7ab1d` are \((D,p,\boldsymbol\theta,Z)=(D_k,p_k,\boldsymbol\theta_k,Z_k)\). Use its original-mass canonical parity selection: with \(\pi_{k,\mathbf b}=\sum_{\mathbf I\equiv\mathbf b\pmod2}p_{k,\mathbf I}\),

\[
q^{\mathrm{can}}_{k,\mathbf J}
=\sum_{\mathbf I:\,\pi_{k,\mathbf I\bmod2}>0}
\frac{p_{k,\mathbf I}p_{k,2\mathbf J-\mathbf I}}{\pi_{k,\mathbf I\bmod2}}.
\]

Write \(p_{\max,k}=\max p_{k,\mathbf I}\) and \(\delta_k=\operatorname{TV}(p_k,q_k^{\mathrm{can}})\), where total variation is one half of the \(\ell^1\) distance. Suppose \(p_{\max,k}\to0\) and \(\delta_k\to0\).

Use exactly the cores and maps of accepted fact `3f23ec160b160e93`: \(\eta_k=\sqrt{p_{\max,k}}\); \(K_k\) is a minimum-area convex hull of a subset carrying original mass at least \(1-\eta_k\); \(F_k=K_k\cap\mathbb Z^2\); and \(\alpha_k=p_k(F_k)\). With its maximum-area triangle vertices \(\mathbf u_{k,0},\mathbf u_{k,1},\mathbf u_{k,2}\), set

\[
\begin{aligned}
G_k&=[\mathbf u_{k,1}-\mathbf u_{k,0}\ \ \mathbf u_{k,2}-\mathbf u_{k,0}],
&\mathbf c_\triangle&=(1/3,1/3),\\
A_k(\mathbf x)&=G_k^{-1}(\mathbf x-\mathbf u_{k,0})-\mathbf c_\triangle,
&\Gamma_k&=G_k^{-1}\mathbb Z^2,\\
\boldsymbol\lambda_k&=G_k^T\boldsymbol\theta_k.
\end{aligned}
\]

Choose \(\mathbf g_{k,1}\) to be a shortest nonzero vector of \(\Gamma_k\), extend it to a basis, and choose \(\mathbf g_{k,2}\) by the nearest-integer reduction specified in `3f23ec160b160e93`. Put \(t_k=|\boldsymbol\lambda_k\cdot\mathbf g_{k,1}|\) and \(c_*=e^{-1}(1-e^{-1})^2\). Then, for all sufficiently large \(k\),

\[
\delta_k+4\eta_k
\ge c_*(1-e^{-t_k})^2e^{-2t_k}
\left[1-\frac{64p_{\max,k}}{1-\eta_k}\right]_+.
\tag{1}
\]

Consequently, for every \(0<\varepsilon<T<\infty\), eventually \(t_k\notin[\varepsilon,T]\). In particular, if the scores \(t_k\) are bounded, then \(t_k\to0\).

The proof also supplies the following finite-law comparison. In any integral affine lattice coordinates \((i,j)\), let \(u\) be a positive log-affine law on the lattice points of a bounded full-dimensional convex polygon \(K\), with score \(t>0\) in the \(j\)-direction. Write \(m_{\ge3}\) for its total mass on lines \(i=\mathrm{constant}\) containing at least three support sites. Its canonical law, with original-mass full two-coordinate parity selection, satisfies

\[
\operatorname{TV}(u,\mathcal T(u))
\ge c_*(1-e^{-t})^2e^{-2t}m_{\ge3}.
\tag{2}
\]

Here \(\mathcal T\) is exactly the canonical operator in `b09fd2c6d7d7ab1d`. Conditioning the original root law on \(F_k\) below is auxiliary; it does not replace the original root in any project atomic moment or root-law assertion. The symbols \(C,S\) retain their locked-problem meanings.
